Breastplate of Judgment
BREST-playt of JUJ-ment
n. phrase
Breastplate from Old English brēost (breast) + plate; Hebrew chōshen ha-mishpāt, the square pouch of intricate work worn over the high priest’s heart, containing the twelve engraved gemstones representing the twelve tribes and the sacred Urim and Thummim.

📖 Biblical Definition

The breastplate of judgment was the square pouch of intricate work worn over the heart of the Old Testament high priest—a piece of cunning workmanship of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen, doubled into a square pouch a span long and a span broad (approximately 9 inches square), bearing twelve engraved gemstones in four rows of three, each stone engraved with the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel, and holding within its pouch the Urim and Thummim. Exodus 28:15-30 prescribes the construction. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the engraved stones: each of the twelve tribes had its name engraved on a particular gemstone (sardius, topaz, carbuncle, emerald, sapphire, diamond, ligure, agate, amethyst, beryl, onyx, jasper), and the stones were set in gold ouches and bound onto the breastplate. The high priest, wearing the breastplate over his heart, bore the names of the twelve tribes upon his heart in the most precious materials. Second, the location: directly over the heart of the high priest, the seat of his deepest affections and his thought-life. Aaron bore the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the LORD continually (Ex 28:29-30)—a permanent symbolic action by which the priestly love-and-thought toward the people was figured in the very materials of his vestment. Third, the function: bearing the names and the judgment (the Urim and Thummim within the pouch) together. The high priest brought the people’s names before the LORD as he ministered, and he sought the LORD’s judgment on the people’s behalf through the Urim and Thummim housed in the same pouch. The breastplate was therefore both representational (the tribes’ names borne before the LORD) and oracular (the means of seeking the LORD’s judgment). Fourth, the typological substance. Christ as our Great High Priest bears the names of His people on His heart perpetually before the Father, and brings before the Father all the judgments that concern His people’s situations and providences. Hebrews 4:14-16, 7:25, 9:24 set the substance: Christ ever lives to make intercession for His people, appearing in the presence of God for them, bearing their names and their cases continually. The breastplate-of-judgment imagery yields one of Scripture’s most tender pastoral pictures: the saint’s name engraved on a precious stone over the heart of the Great High Priest, perpetually before the Father, with every providence and decision concerning the saint being brought before the throne through the High Priest who is touched with the feeling of every infirmity.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BREASTPLATE as a piece of defensive armor for the breast; in scripture, the square pouch of cunning workmanship over the high priest’s heart, bearing the twelve engraved gemstones of the tribes and containing the Urim and Thummim, by which the priest bore the judgment of the people before the LORD continually.

BREASTPLATE, n. — 1. Armor for the breast. 2. Among the Jews, a part of the vestment of the high priest, consisting of a square pouch worn on the breast, set with twelve precious stones, on which were engraved the names of the twelve tribes (Ex 28:15-30).

JUDGMENT, n. — 1. The act of judging; the act or process of the mind in comparing its ideas. 2. A decision or determination of any mind on what is presented to it. In scripture, the divine decisions of the LORD on the cases of His people brought before Him.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 28:15-17 — "And thou shalt make the breastplate of judgment with cunning work; after the work of the ephod thou shalt make it; of gold, of blue, and of purple, and of scarlet, and of fine twined linen, shalt thou make it. Foursquare it shall be being doubled; a span shall be the length thereof, and a span shall be the breadth thereof. And thou shalt set in it settings of stones..."

Exodus 28:29-30 — "And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually. And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron’s heart..."

Hebrews 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Hebrews 4:15-16 — "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The breastplate-of-judgment doctrine is corrupted, in much contemporary preaching, by the general loss of priestly typology that no longer traces the high priest’s vestments to their Christological fulfillment—and by the consequent loss of one of Scripture’s most tender pastoral pictures: the saint’s name engraved on a precious stone perpetually over the heart of the Great High Priest who bears every providence concerning the saint before the Father.

expand to see more

The breastplate of judgment is one of several Old Testament priestly typologies that contemporary preaching tends to skip past as ancient cultic detail without tracing the substantive pastoral connections the typology supplies. The image is unusually tender: the high priest of God’s people wore over his heart twelve precious stones, each engraved with one of the tribe’s names; he bore those names continually before the LORD; he carried within the same breastplate the Urim and Thummim by which the people’s judgments could be sought. Each tribe had its place on his heart; each tribe’s name was inscribed in the most precious of materials; each tribe’s case was brought before the LORD through the same priestly office. The Christological substance is direct. Christ as the Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His heart before the Father; each name is precious to Him; each case concerning each name is brought before the Father through His intercession; not one of His people is forgotten. The recovery is the recovery of the typology and its pastoral substance.

The pastoral application is one of the deepest in Scripture for the believer who struggles with the question whether the Lord remembers him. The breastplate-of-judgment doctrine answers: the Great High Priest has your name engraved upon a precious stone over His own heart, perpetually before the Father; He bears your judgment—your cases, your providences, your decisions, your trials—before the throne continually; you are not forgotten, not absent from His remembrance, not omitted from His intercession. Hebrews 7:25 closes the circle: he ever liveth to make intercession for them. The High Priest’s breastplate is, in its New Covenant fulfillment, the heart of Christ, on which every redeemed saint’s name is engraved in the most precious of materials forever. The contemporary believer who has not seen this picture has missed one of Scripture’s most tender pastoral consolations; the recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of confidence that the Great High Priest knows His sheep by name and bears them perpetually before the Father in the very place where atonement was eternally accomplished.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chōshen ha-mishpāt (breastplate of judgment); the square pouch of cunning workmanship over the high priest’s heart, bearing the twelve engraved gemstones of the tribes and containing the Urim and Thummim; typologically fulfilled in Christ the Great High Priest who bears His people’s names on His heart perpetually before the Father and intercedes for them continually.

expand to see more

Hebrew chōshen (H2833) — breastplate, pouch (over 25 OT uses, almost all in Exodus and Leviticus of the high priest’s breastplate).

Hebrew mishpāt (H4941) — judgment (the second element of the compound).

Hebrew ephod (H646) — ephod (the priestly vestment over which the breastplate was worn).

Greek entugchánō (G1793) — to intercede (the verb of Christ’s priestly intercession in Heb 7:25; Rom 8:34).

Usage

"The breastplate of judgment bore the names of the twelve tribes engraved on twelve precious stones, over the high priest’s heart, before the LORD continually."

"Christ as the Great High Priest perpetually bears the names of His people on His heart before the Father—the breastplate-of-judgment’s typological fulfillment."

"The pastoral consolation is direct: each saint’s name is engraved on a precious stone over the heart of the Christ who ever lives to make intercession for him."
